units.t: Art History. Episode two.
In this episode: The day the Mona Lisa vanished, Michelangelo and the Sistine Chapel ceiling, Vermeer: the mystery of light and The Great Wave and the floating world.
Part one. The day the Mona Lisa vanished.
In 1911 a handyman walked out of the Louvre with the world's most famous painting under his smock.
Strangely, the theft is a big part of why it became so famous.
A quiet Monday.
Mondays were cleaning days at the Louvre.
The galleries were shut and workmen wandered the halls.
On the morning of 21 August 1911, a man in a white workman's smock lifted Leonardo da Vinci's portrait off its hooks in the Salon Carré.
The painting is small, about 77 by 53 centimetres, and painted on a thin poplar panel rather than canvas.
The thief carried it to a service stairwell, removed the heavy frame and protective glass box, and slipped the panel under his clothing.
Accounts differ on whether he hid in a storeroom overnight or arrived that morning among the staff.
Either way, he walked out into the Paris streets and nobody stopped him.
Nobody noticed.
The next morning, the painter Louis Béroud arrived to sketch and found four iron pegs where the Mona Lisa should have been.
Guards assumed the museum's photographers had taken it, which happened regularly.
Only when Béroud pressed them did the truth sink in.
The Louvre closed for a week and the director lost his job.
Police followed strange trails.
The poet Guillaume Apollinaire was jailed for several days because an acquaintance had earlier stolen ancient statuettes from the Louvre that Picasso had ended up with.
Picasso was questioned too.
Both were cleared.
The real thief had been interviewed early, at his lodgings, and aroused no suspicion.
The inside man.
Vincenzo Peruggia was an Italian craftsman who had worked at the Louvre and helped install the very glass cases meant to protect its paintings.
He knew the building, and the staff knew him.
For more than two years he kept the Mona Lisa in a trunk with a false bottom in his Paris room.
In late 1913 he wrote to Alfredo Geri, an art dealer in Florence, offering to return the painting to Italy.
Geri arranged a hotel meeting with Giovanni Poggi, director of the Uffizi Gallery.
After examining the panel and checking the Louvre's markings on its back, they alerted police, and Peruggia was arrested.
Patriot or opportunist.
At his trial in Florence, Peruggia argued that he had acted out of patriotism.
He believed, wrongly, that Napoleon had looted the painting from Italy.
In fact Leonardo took it to France himself, and it entered the French royal collection long before Napoleon was born.
Peruggia's story struck a chord with many Italians, and he received a fairly light sentence of a little over a year, of which he served only about seven months.
Historians note that he had also asked for money, so his motives were probably mixed.
Before going home, the painting was displayed in Florence, Rome and Milan to enormous crowds.
It returned to the Louvre in early 1914.
How theft made a star.
Before 1911, the Mona Lisa was admired by art lovers, but it was not obviously the most famous painting on Earth.
The theft changed that.
For two years the story ran in newspapers worldwide, and photographs of the portrait were printed again and again.
Visitors even queued at the Louvre to stare at the empty space on the wall.
When the painting came back, it returned as a celebrity.
Art historians often call the theft a turning point, alongside Leonardo's reputation and the picture's remarkable technique, such as the soft, smoky blending called sfumato.
Today it sits behind protective glass and is seen by millions of visitors every year.
The key idea: The Mona Lisa was stolen on Monday 21 August 1911, when the Louvre was closed for cleaning and workmen moved freely.
Part two. Michelangelo and the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
A sculptor who didn't want the job spent four years painting a chapel ceiling twenty metres above the floor.
He didn't do it lying on his back, either.
A reluctant painter.
In 1508, Michelangelo Buonarroti was in his early thirties and already famous for his marble David in Florence and his Pietà in Rome.
He thought of himself first as a sculptor.
Pope Julius II, a forceful and warlike pope, had hired him to carve a grand tomb, but then turned to decorating the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, built by his uncle, Pope Sixtus IV.
Michelangelo had little experience of fresco and accepted reluctantly.
The walls already held frescoes by leading painters such as Botticelli and Perugino.
The ceiling, painted as a starry sky, was about to be transformed.
Painting on wet plaster.
Fresco means fresh in Italian.
The painter applies pigments mixed with water onto wet lime plaster.
As the plaster dries, a chemical reaction locks the colour into the wall, making it extremely durable.
The catch is speed.
Each day only as much plaster as could be painted before it set was laid.
These daily patches are called giornate, from the Italian for a day's work.
Mistakes could not be painted over; the plaster had to be chipped away and redone.
Michelangelo's team transferred his designs to the plaster using full-size drawings called cartoons, either by pricking holes along the lines or by pressing them into the soft surface.
Standing, not lying down.
A popular image shows Michelangelo lying on his back for years, paint dripping onto his face.
In reality, he designed a wooden scaffold that bridged the chapel just below the ceiling, leaving the floor free for services.
He and his assistants worked standing, heads tilted back and arms raised.
It was still punishing.
Michelangelo wrote a comic poem, with a little sketch in the margin, complaining about his aching neck, bent back and the paint dripping onto his face.
Nor did he work entirely alone, as another myth claims.
Assistants ground pigments, prepared plaster and helped with some painting, although he painted the great majority of the figures himself.
The story overhead.
The ceiling is about 40 metres long and 13 metres wide, with more than 300 figures.
Down the centre run nine scenes from Genesis, from God separating light from darkness to the story of Noah.
Around them sit huge prophets and sibyls, prophetesses from the classical world, and muscular nude youths called ignudi on painted architecture that only looks three-dimensional.
Michelangelo painted the scenes in reverse story order, starting near the entrance with Noah, and his figures grew larger as he went.
In The Creation of Adam, fingertips almost meet.
Some writers say the shape around God resembles a brain, hidden by Michelangelo the anatomist, but there is no evidence he intended it.
Judgment and restoration.
The ceiling was unveiled in 1512 and stunned everyone who saw it.
More than two decades later, Michelangelo painted The Last Judgment across the wall behind the altar, working from 1536 to 1541.
Christ raises the saved while the damned tumble towards hell.
Some church officials were scandalised by the nudity, and after his death Daniele da Volterra was hired to paint drapery over figures, earning the nickname Il Braghettone, the breeches maker.
For centuries, candle and incense smoke and old varnish darkened the ceiling.
A Vatican restoration from 1980 to 1994 revealed vivid pinks, greens, oranges and blues.
It was controversial, with some critics arguing that final touches were lost.
The chapel still hosts the conclave that elects a pope.
The key idea: Pope Julius II hired Michelangelo, who saw himself as a sculptor, to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling in 1508.
Part three. Vermeer: the mystery of light.
Barely three dozen paintings, almost no letters, no surviving drawings.
Johannes Vermeer painted quiet rooms full of light, and art detectives are still arguing about how he did it.
Few paintings, fewer records.
Johannes Vermeer was baptised in Delft, in the Dutch Republic, in 1632.
His father was a weaver who also dealt in art, and Johannes took over the business.
He married Catharina Bolnes, from a Catholic family, in 1653, and they had a large family.
He joined the painters' guild and later served as one of its heads.
Yet he left no diaries, no letters about his art and no drawing that can confidently be attributed to him.
Nearly everything known comes from legal and financial documents.
Scholars attribute only about 34 to 37 surviving paintings to him, and some attributions are disputed.
He seems to have worked very slowly, perhaps finishing only a few a year.
Light from the left.
A striking number of Vermeer's paintings show a quiet room lit by a window on the left.
The figures are usually one or two women, reading letters, pouring milk, playing music or weighing pearls.
A local collector, Pieter van Ruijven, appears to have bought many of them, which may have let Vermeer work carefully.
He watched how daylight behaves.
In The Milkmaid, the whitewashed wall is full of subtle shifts, tiny nail holes and marks.
Shadows are not just darker; they pick up colour from nearby surfaces.
Tiny dots of light paint suggest sparkle on bread, metal or fabric.
They resemble the blurred highlights of an out-of-focus lens, which has fuelled debate about his methods.
Expensive blue.
Natural ultramarine was made from lapis lazuli, a semi-precious stone mined in what is now Afghanistan.
It cost more than many other pigments, and many painters saved it for important details, such as the robes of the Virgin Mary.
Vermeer used it remarkably freely.
It appears in the blue and yellow headscarf of the Girl with a Pearl Earring and in the apron of The Milkmaid.
Technical studies have also found ultramarine mixed into shadows and underlayers, where it helps create cool, luminous tones.
Such lavish spending is puzzling for an artist who ended his life in debt.
It remains part of the mystery of his methods and his finances.
The camera obscura debate.
A camera obscura is a darkened box or room in which a lens projects an image of the outside scene onto a surface.
The device was known in Vermeer's day.
Delft was home to the microscope pioneer Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, later trustee of Vermeer's bankrupt estate, though nothing suggests they discussed optics.
In 2001 the historian Philip Steadman argued that the geometry of several Vermeer rooms fits a camera obscura, and David Hockney suggested Old Masters used optical aids.
In the 2013 documentary Tim's Vermeer, inventor Tim Jenison used a lens and mirror to produce a strikingly close copy of The Music Lesson without painting training.
Critics reply that possible is not proven.
No document mentions Vermeer owning such a device, and composition, colour and mood still demanded his skill.
Lost and found.
In 1672 France invaded the Dutch Republic and the art market collapsed.
Vermeer's income dried up.
He died in December 1675, aged 43, leaving his family deeply in debt.
His widow later said the stress of financial ruin had contributed to his death.
Over the following centuries his name faded, and some paintings were sold under other artists' names.
In the 1860s the French critic Théophile Thoré-Bürger published enthusiastic articles about him and helped restore his reputation.
Since then his fame has soared.
The Girl with a Pearl Earring is now one of the best-known paintings in the world, and a major Vermeer exhibition in Amsterdam in 2023 sold out completely.
The key idea: Vermeer left only about 34 to 37 paintings and almost no personal records, so much about him is guesswork.
Part four. The Great Wave and the floating world.
A giant wave curls like a claw over three tiny boats while Mount Fuji sits calmly in the distance.
This Japanese print is one of the most famous images on Earth.
Here is the world that made it.
Pictures of the floating world.
During the Edo period, from 1603 to 1868, Japan was largely closed to the outside world and ruled from Edo, today's Tokyo.
As cities grew, prosperous merchants and artisans built a lively popular culture of theatre, teahouses, fashion and pleasure districts.
The word 'ukiyo' once meant a sorrowful, fleeting world in a Buddhist sense, but came to mean the 'floating world' of urban entertainment, enjoyed for the moment.
Ukiyo-e, pictures of the floating world, showed that culture.
Early ones were paintings, but woodblock prints made them affordable to ordinary townspeople.
Popular subjects included kabuki actors, celebrated beauties and courtesans, legendary heroes and, later, landscapes and travel scenes.
They were the posters and celebrity photos of their day.
A team effort.
We usually name a single artist, but a ukiyo-e print was a team product.
The publisher came up with the project, paid for it and sold the results.
The designer, the artist we remember, drew the image in ink on thin paper.
A skilled carver pasted that drawing face down onto a block of cherry wood and carved away everything except the lines, destroying the original in the process.
Extra blocks were carved for each colour.
A printer then brushed water-based ink onto each block in turn and pressed damp paper onto it by hand with a flat pad called a baren.
Small notches called kento made sure each colour lined up precisely.
A single print could need a dozen or more blocks.
Brocade pictures.
Early woodblock prints were black and white or had a few colours added by hand.
In 1765 the artist Suzuki Harunobu and his collaborators produced prints using many separate colour blocks, made possible by the reliable registration system.
These full-colour prints were called nishiki-e, or 'brocade pictures', because their rich colours reminded people of luxurious woven silk.
They kicked off a golden age.
Kitagawa Utamaro became famous for elegant portraits of women, often close-up half-length figures.
Toshusai Sharaku produced striking, almost caricature-like portraits of kabuki actors in a career of less than a year, before vanishing from the record.
Prints were produced in large editions and sold in shops, many relatively cheaply, part of the everyday visual life of the city.
Hokusai and Hiroshige.
Katsushika Hokusai, born in 1760, worked for roughly seven decades and changed his name around thirty times.
Around 1831 he designed Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji.
Its most famous image, Under the Wave off Kanagawa, now called The Great Wave, shows boats dwarfed by a towering wave whose foam breaks into claw-like fingers, with Fuji small in the distance.
It uses Prussian blue, an imported synthetic pigment cheaper and more lasting than earlier blues.
Thousands of copies were probably printed.
His younger rival Utagawa Hiroshige became famous for gentler, atmospheric landscapes.
His 1830s series The Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido followed the road from Edo to Kyoto through rain, snow and dusk, part souvenir and part journey for those who could not travel.
Soft colour gradations, made by wiping the ink on the block, put viewers in the scene.
Japan meets Europe.
In the 1850s Japan was forced to open its ports to foreign trade, and Japanese goods flowed into Europe.
A popular story says a French artist found Hokusai's sketches used as packing around porcelain; it may be partly legend, but prints certainly arrived in large numbers.
Japonisme swept through Western art and design.
Artists admired bold flat colour, strong outlines, unusual high or low viewpoints and off-centre compositions, which differed from Europe's realistic perspective.
Van Gogh and his brother Theo collected hundreds of prints in Paris, and Vincent painted copies of two Hiroshige prints with his own intense colours.
Monet's collection still hangs at Giverny, and his Japanese-style footbridge appears in his garden paintings.
Degas and Cassatt borrowed the cropped, off-centre compositions.
The floating world helped shape modern Western art.
The key idea: Ukiyo-e were affordable woodblock prints celebrating the urban pleasures of Edo-period Japan.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why could the thief move so freely through the Louvre?
Answer. The galleries were closed and workmen were about.
Question two. How did Michelangelo see himself when he accepted the commission?
Answer. First of all as a sculptor, new to fresco.
Question three. What makes Vermeer unusual for a famous painter?
Answer. He left few paintings and almost no personal records.
Question four. What made ukiyo-e affordable to ordinary townspeople?
Answer. Many copies could be printed from the same blocks.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
